evidence: relations.py:61 defines verify_base_tables(connection, sql, *, dialect) so a positional conn and keyword dialect work. It handles dialect=="mysql" at lines 76 and 102. It calls connection.cursor() at line 73, which pymysql connections provide. sql_runner.py:12 imports it and line 125 calls it as claimed.

verify_base_tables (relations.py:61-137) uses a plain connection.cursor() with %s-parameterized pg_catalog query (lines 91-97), fetchone, and closes it in finally (133). It is called at sql_runner.py:155, after the SET statement_timeout setup cursor (closed) and before the named cursor is created at 161. psycopg2 named cursors (DECLARE ... CURSOR) need only an open transaction; prior statements in the same implicit transaction are fine, and this just reuses it. Read-only set_session happens before any statement (141). Failures are wrapped into RlsError (fail-closed). Not run against a live Postgres.

sql_runner.py:126 passes a sqlite3.Connection. relations.py:73 uses connection.cursor(), and the sqlite branch (line 86) calls _sqlite_kind, which runs 'SELECT type FROM pragma_table_list(?) WHERE schema = ?' (lines 151-154). That function exists from SQLite 3.37. If it is unavailable, sqlite3.OperationalError is raised, caught by the generic handler at lines 136-137, and re-raised as RlsError, so the query is blocked (fail closed). I did not run it against a live SQLite build.

sql_runner.py:93-143. The connection is freshly opened (96) with default isolation_level, so no transaction is open when conn.execute('BEGIN') runs at 125. The earlier PRAGMA query_only statements (108-109) do not open a transaction, and the progress handler does not either. In legacy sqlite3 mode, Python only issues an implicit BEGIN before DML when not already in a transaction, so cursor.execute(args.sql) after the explicit BEGIN does not issue a second BEGIN. Read path: returns at 133 with no commit, and conn.close() at 143 rolls back the open transaction, which is harmless for a read. Write path: conn.commit() at 135 commits the explicit transaction. Exceptions from verify_base_tables are cleaned up by the finally block, since close rolls back. BEGIN is allowed under query_only. The only way to get a nested-BEGIN error is user SQL that is itself BEGIN, which is not a normal input and was already an error before this change.

All six concrete SqlRunner subclasses under src/ declare `*, require_base_tables: bool = False` in run_sql: RowCapRunner (safety/limits.py:84), ReadOnlyGuardRunner (safety/__init__.py:81), RlsGuardRunner (safety/__init__.py:146), PostgresRunner (postgres/sql_runner.py:106), SqliteRunner (sqlite/sql_runner.py:73), MySQLRunner (mysql/sql_runner.py:73). safety/__init__.py:185-193 uses inspect.signature(runner.run_sql).parameters and accepts if 'require_base_tables' is named or any VAR_KEYWORD exists; AttributeError/TypeError/ValueError fail closed. Standard-library behaviour: MagicMock/AsyncMock attributes expose (*args, **kwargs), so VAR_KEYWORD makes them accepted (true accept, since they take any kwarg); functools.wraps functions are followed via __wrapped__; a callable-object run_sql is introspected via its __call__. ReadOnlyGuardRunner (safety/__init__.py:107-108) and RowCapRunner (safety/limits.py:88-89) forward require_base_tables to inner. SQLite runs conn.execute('BEGIN') (deferred, read-only type) before verify, and the first catalog read takes the read snapshot that the query then shares. relations.py:61-137 has no cache or lru_cache, and the docstring says so; catalog lookups run fresh per call. Absolute claim traced: a repeated call with the same SQL re-executes the catalog queries.

relations.py verify_base_tables: views/matviews (kinds view,v,m,VIEW,SYSTEM VIEW) raise RlsError (124-127); unknown kinds raise RlsError (128-131); unsupported shapes raise RlsError in _relations (47,57); catalog/driver failures are caught by `except Exception` and re-raised as RlsError (136-137), since the cursor.execute calls are inside the outer try (69). So a driver error does not escape raw. Tables (table,r,p,BASE TABLE) pass through. Only exception is _METADATA_VIEWS allowlist (relations.py:100,105), which the doc states on line 43 of row-level-security.md directly after the claim line 41.

relations.py:20-35: postgres set is information_schema {schemata,tables,columns,views,table_constraints,key_column_usage,referential_constraints,constraint_column_usage,check_constraints} plus pg_catalog {pg_tables,pg_views,pg_indexes}. mysql set is information_schema {schemata,tables,columns,views,statistics,table_constraints,key_column_usage,referential_constraints,check_constraints}. pg_stats and COLUMN_STATISTICS are absent. This matches doc line 43. Matching keys are (namespace,name), lowercased for MySQL (lines 100,105-107). Minor imprecision: external doc line 161 says MySQL has 'the same' views as PostgreSQL plus statistics, but the MySQL set omits constraint_column_usage (a view MySQL does not have). That is not a defect in the claim.

relations.py:91-101: postgres runs to_regclass, selects relkind, nspname and relname, and exempts a view only if (nspname, relname) is in _METADATA_VIEWS['postgres']. A user view `columns` in another schema resolves to a different nspname and is refused (line 124). relations.py:105-108: MySQL exempts only when (relation.db.lower(), relation.name.lower()) is in the set, with no catalog query. Traced input: an unqualified `columns` gives db '' and does not match, so it falls through to the TABLE_TYPE lookup and is refused if it is a view. `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS` matches case-insensitively. The claim that MySQL refuses to create objects in information_schema is an external fact and is not checked in code.

relations.py:151-158 _sqlite_kind queries pragma_table_list (added in SQLite 3.37) and returns its type. Only 'table' passes (line 128). It is a real table, not unavailable metadata, so it does not contradict the claim.

postgres/sql_runner.py:60-67,126,155 uses psycopg2 and passes the raw psycopg2 connection to verify_base_tables. psycopg2 uses pyformat (%s) with tuple params. relations.py:73 calls connection.cursor() with the default tuple cursor, so row[0] indexing is valid. relations.py:99-131: for postgres kind=relkind. Line 128 passes only 'r' and 'p' (plus other dialects' values). Line 124 rejects 'v' and 'm' as views. Any other relkind (f, t, i, S, c) or None fails the line 128 check and is blocked. The only exception is a 'v' in _METADATA_VIEWS (line 100), a documented allowlist for system views, which doesn't change the claim's relkind classification.

MySQL documents information_schema.TABLES.TABLE_TYPE as BASE TABLE, VIEW or SYSTEM VIEW (the last for INFORMATION_SCHEMA tables). This matches relations.py:124-131, which treats VIEW and SYSTEM VIEW as views and BASE TABLE as accepted. I am relying on the MySQL documentation from memory and did not re-read it in this session. MariaDB adds extra values such as SEQUENCE, SYSTEM VERSIONED and TEMPORARY. Those fall to the `kind not in (...)` check at line 128 and raise RlsError, so the guard blocks the query and does not let it through. The claim is about MySQL, so that does not contradict it.

relations.py:76-81 runs SELECT @@lower_case_table_names, requires mode[0] in (0,1,2) else raises RlsError (fails closed), and sets mysql_fold = mode[0] != 0. MySQL docs: 0 = case-sensitive comparison, 1 = stored lowercase and compared case-insensitively, 2 = stored as given but compared lowercase; so non-zero means folding. The runner uses pymysql (sql_runner.py:50), whose text protocol decoders convert integer columns (the variable is an integer-typed system var) to Python int. This is from knowledge of pymysql; I did not run it against a server. If a driver returned str or bytes, the code would fail closed rather than misreport.

relations.py:75-81 reads @@lower_case_table_names and sets mysql_fold for modes 1 and 2, rejecting any value outside 0, 1 or 2. Lines 109-117 compare BINARY TABLE_SCHEMA with BINARY COALESCE(%s, DATABASE()) and BINARY TABLE_NAME with BINARY %s. When mysql_fold is set, LOWER() wraps both sides of each comparison (111-113). Mode 0 gives an exact byte-wise case-sensitive match, which is MySQL's own rule. Mode 1 stores names lowercase and compares them case-insensitively. Mode 2 stores names as given and compares them case-insensitively. LOWER on both sides with BINARY matches both of those. BINARY only forces byte comparison, which overrides the information_schema column collation. It is deprecated in MySQL 8.0.27+ only as a CAST shorthand, so it still works and gives at most a warning. Known edge: LOWER() is not exactly the filesystem's case folding for exotic Unicode names, which is minor. I did not run this against a live MySQL server.

relations.py:151-157 runs SELECT type FROM pragma_table_list(?) WHERE schema = ?. SQLite's PRAGMA table_list (3.37+) returns columns schema, name, type, ncol, wr and strict. type is one of table, view, shadow or virtual. It is exposed as a table-valued function with the table name as its argument. This rests on SQLite's documented behavior. I did not run it, and I did not check the sqlite3 version the runner uses. On SQLite older than 3.37 the query would error, but the code turns that into RlsError, which blocks the query.

relations.py:144-145 reads row[1] from PRAGMA database_list, whose columns are (seq, name, file), so index 1 is the schema name. The schema list is temp, then main, then the remaining attached schemas in database_list order (seq order, i.e. attach order). That matches SQLite's documented unqualified-name resolution: temp, then main, then attached databases in attach order. If temp also appears in database_list it is only a harmless duplicate lookup. This rests on SQLite's documented behavior, not on a run.

verify_base_tables has only three call sites, all passing the live per-query connection: postgres/sql_runner.py:155 (psycopg2 conn from connect, same conn used for cursors), mysql/sql_runner.py:125 (pymysql conn), sqlite/sql_runner.py:126 (sqlite3 conn, after BEGIN). All are DB-API connections exposing cursor(); relations.py:73-133 uses cursor.execute/fetchone/close (no fetchall found in use, which is a subset of the claim). RlsGuardRunner and limits wrappers (safety/__init__.py:179, limits.py:88) don't call verify_base_tables; they only forward require_base_tables to the inner runner, which then uses its own live connection. sqlite3.Connection.cursor() is standard DB-API.

relations.py:61-137. No cache: verify_base_tables opens a fresh cursor and queries the catalog per call, with no module-level or persistent state (the only module state is the constant _METADATA_VIEWS). Views refused: the postgres branch (91-101) skips only views whose resolved (nspname, relname) is in the allowlist and otherwise raises on kind 'v' or 'm' (124-127). Trace for pg_stats: it is relkind 'v', not in the allowlist, so it is refused. The mysql branch (105-107) skips only listed information_schema names. Trace for information_schema.COLUMN_STATISTICS: it is not listed, the TABLES lookup returns 'SYSTEM VIEW', and it is refused (124). The sqlite branch returns the type from pragma_table_list, so 'view' is refused. Unknown kinds, failed lookups and unsupported dialects are refused (123, 128-137). Table-valued functions and odd relation shapes raise in _relations (46-47, 56-57). The sqlite_master family is treated as a table; it is a real table, not a view. I did not search the runner or connector wrappers for caching.

relations.py:20-35 _METADATA_VIEWS contains neither pg_stats nor COLUMN_STATISTICS. Postgres path (lines 91-101): pg_stats is relkind 'v' in pg_catalog, not allowlisted, so it falls to line 124 and raises RlsError. MySQL path (105-127): COLUMN_STATISTICS is not allowlisted, so it is looked up in information_schema.TABLES. It is a SYSTEM VIEW, so line 124 refuses it, and an unknown kind is refused at line 128. The claim covers only the absence and blocking of the stats views, and the code matches. The separate 'structure not rows' wording is not what this claim asserts. Views like check_constraints and views expose definition SQL, but that is not the claimed property.

relations.py:102-108: the allowlist check lowercases relation.db and name and matches only ('information_schema', name) in _METADATA_VIEWS['mysql'] (lines 29-34). An unqualified name has db '' so it never matches and goes to the catalog lookup (109-121). In MySQL/MariaDB, information_schema is a server-managed read-only schema that cannot hold user objects, and its names resolve case-insensitively. I checked this against general knowledge of MySQL, not against a documentation file in the repo. The comment is accurate. The absolute-claim input I traced is an unqualified allowlisted name, which falls through to the lookup as described.

relations.py:91-101: the query joins pg_class to pg_namespace on c.oid = to_regclass(name), so the exemption is checked against the real nspname of the relation the live connection resolved (same connection/search_path as execution, per the docstring at 64-65). A user view shadowing an unqualified name via search_path resolves to its own schema and is not in _METADATA_VIEWS (lines 20-28), so it is refused as a view at line 124. Trying to falsify with a user schema named pg_catalog: the pg_ prefix is reserved and pg_catalog and information_schema already exist, so a user schema cannot take those names. Absolute-claim input traced: a user view public.tables with search_path=public,information_schema. It resolves to (public, tables), which is not allowlisted, so it is blocked.

rls.py:183-195: for postgres only, quoted identifiers are left untouched (distinction preserved); unquoted ASCII identifiers are lowercased (matches PG's ASCII fold); unquoted non-ASCII identifiers raise RlsError rather than being folded, consistent with the comment that non-ASCII folding depends on server encoding/locale. Traced input: unquoted 'Éa' -> rejected; unquoted 'Foo' -> 'foo'; quoted "Foo" -> unchanged. Docstring and comment match the behavior.

rls.py:183-195 normalize_rls_identifiers mutates identifiers in place (identifier.set) and only for postgres. It skips quoted identifiers and lowercases unquoted ones, which is idempotent. The non-ASCII check raises only for unquoted identifiers, and generated SQL quotes those, so the second pass in relations.py:40 cannot newly fail on pass-1 output. apply_rls calls it at rls.py:227 before predicates are injected at rls.py:287. Injected columns from exp.column (rls.py:164) are not normalized in pass 1. When the rewritten SQL is reparsed, quoting is preserved (to_identifier quotes unsafe names) and unquoted ones get Postgres-correct lowercase folding in pass 2. I did not run the code. This rests on reading sqlglot's to_identifier behavior from memory, not on its source in the views. The two passes run on separate trees, with a re-render and reparse between them, so no double-application effect arises.

relations.py:91-99 selects c.relkind, n.nspname, c.relname and reads row[0], row[1:3]; test mock returns (kind,'public','Orders') in that order (test_rls_views.py:99). relations.py:61-73: verify_base_tables calls _relations first and returns at line 71-72 if empty, before connection.cursor() at line 73. _relations (38-58) only adds scope.sources entries that are exp.Table; a CTE reference resolves to a Scope, not a Table, and the CTE body 'SELECT 1 AS id' has no tables. relations.py:124-127 raises 'database views are not supported...' (contains 'view') for kinds view/v/m/VIEW/SYSTEM VIEW; the generic message at 128-131 ('could not verify a base table') lacks 'view'. Postgres: matviews are relkind 'm' and views 'v', both reach the view branch; pg_stats is relkind 'v' in pg_catalog and is not in the postgres allowlist (relations.py:27 lists only pg_tables, pg_views, pg_indexes), so line 100 does not skip it. MySQL: views give TABLE_TYPE 'VIEW'; COLUMN_STATISTICS is absent from the mysql allowlist (lines 23-31 region) and reports TABLE_TYPE 'SYSTEM VIEW' in MySQL 8 information_schema.TABLES (from MySQL behavior, not run live), which is in the view tuple. The tests at test_connectors.py:101,166 match 'view'. Live DB was not run. A MariaDB server, which lacks COLUMN_STATISTICS, would hit the generic branch, but the fixture is MySQL.

factory.py:198-253 build_sql_runner has read_only: bool = True default and passes read_only to SqliteRunner/PostgresRunner/MySQLRunner. Runners apply read-only session enforcement only when self._read_only is true (postgres sql_runner.py:130-141, mysql :105-111, sqlite :93-101), so read_only=False leaves no driver-level block on DDL; non-read-shaped SQL takes a separate execution path (postgres :157). All three runners' run_sql accept require_base_tables (postgres :107, mysql :74, sqlite :74).

relations.py:124-131: kinds view/v/m/VIEW/SYSTEM VIEW raise the view message; anything not in table/r/p/BASE TABLE raises 'could not verify a base table'. _sqlite_kind (140-158) returns the pragma_table_list type column. SQLite documents that column as table/view/shadow/virtual, so an FTS5 table returns 'virtual' (based on SQLite docs, not run here), which is outside both sets and takes the base-table branch. The test at tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:169-179 expects match='base table', consistent with that.
